body: THE FAULTS GENERATORS MAKE MOST (learned from 650 real clips) – write against them: (1) people in a group never move as copies: different strides, glances and timing, some stand still. (2) A hand really holds its object: fingers closed round it, the object moves with the hand and has weight; a foot, a wheel or a bottle presses on the surface it stands on. (3) Every object keeps its identity: the same phone, cup handle, scarf pattern and number of parts in every second. (4) Light has one direction: shadows and reflections follow their owners and the same lamps. (5) When the camera moves, near things pass faster than far ones and the surroundings stay rigid. (6) Add nothing the request did not ask for: no extra people, steam, flames or objects.

THE FAULTS GENERATORS MAKE MOST – write against them: people in a group differ in pose, height, clothes and where they look; a hand really grips its object with closed fingers and visible weight; every object is whole and correct (right number of parts, one clear shape); light has one direction, so shadows and reflections match their owners; near and far things have natural sharpness; add nothing the request did not ask for.

AI MISTAKE: Everyone in a group steps, turns, looks, or gestures on the same beat, as though one motion were copied across every subject. IN REALITY: People occupy different positions, take different stride lengths, pause to look around, and begin reacting at different moments. Even performers following a shared rhythm show small differences in timing and gesture. Birds on water turn and paddle independently; nearby leaves do not sway in perfect lockstep. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Show a group with loosely coordinated activity, not synchronized duplicates: varied strides, staggered glances and gestures, brief individual pauses, and subjects that remain still while others move.

AI MISTAKE: Fingers hover beside an object, pass through it, change position abruptly, or make a working motion without affecting the material. IN REALITY: A held cup stays against the same gripping fingers until the grip adjusts or releases. Fingertips press lightly into soft surfaces. A blade meets the bread it cuts, and a separated slice remains where it passed; folded paper keeps its crease. Small objects remain distinct from the hands carrying them. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Keep hand anatomy and grip continuous. Show visible contact, slight pressure, and the corresponding change in the object at each push, fold, cut, or handoff.

AI MISTAKE: Reflections look pasted onto the frame, show the wrong source, or remain perfectly sharp and fixed when a surface, light, or viewpoint changes. IN REALITY: Ripples break a reflected lamp into moving fragments; rough wet pavement spreads highlights into blurred patches. A reflection on tilted glass shifts with the glass and the viewing angle, while a passing light appears and fades in the appropriate place. Different surfaces distort reflections differently. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Match each reflected highlight to a visible light source, surface shape, and camera angle. Let water fragment reflections, wet ground blur them, and moving glass carry changing highlights.

AI MISTAKE: The scene gains extra pedestrians, signs, weather, landmarks, or dramatic activity merely because a location label or offscreen sound suggests them. IN REALITY: A quiet roadside view can stay sparsely occupied. A kitchen close-up can show only hands preparing food, without added splashes or other activity. Traffic heard beyond a room does not require a visible vehicle, and a wide landscape can remain empty. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Include only subjects, objects, and events established in the described view. Preserve the original framing and level of activity; do not turn implied context or offscreen sound into new visible scene content.

AI MISTAKE: A prop changes shape, markings, count, or position between frames even though nothing happens to alter it. IN REALITY: A cup handle stays on the same side of the cup as it turns; a phone retains its dimensions and camera layout. A scarf pattern moves with its fabric rather than rearranging itself. Stationary furniture and wall details keep their positions, while carried objects follow continuous paths through the shot. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Preserve each object's recognizable geometry, markings, and small features across continuous frames. Let perspective change their appearance naturally, but show any change of position through an observable movement or interaction.

AI MISTAKE: Every part of the scene is equally readable, with dark interiors lifted to match bright openings and little difference between sunlit and shaded surfaces. IN REALITY: A bright doorway can lose visible detail while nearby fabric remains dim. Faces turned away from a window stay darker than those facing it, and a low sun can leave foreground figures in silhouette. Lamps illuminate nearby areas more strongly than distant corners. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Keep the lighting range grounded in the actual sources. Allow bright openings to wash out, retain deep but legible shadows where appropriate, and vary surface brightness according to orientation, distance, and obstruction.

AI MISTAKE: Shadows drift away from their objects, highlights jump between surfaces, or exposure and color change without a corresponding change in lighting or viewpoint. IN REALITY: Under steady sunlight, a moving seat carries its shadow along a consistent direction. A desk lamp brightens the work area nearest its beam while surrounding surfaces remain dimmer. Window light can make the opening very bright and leave a nearby panel dark; turning a surface changes how strongly it catches that light. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Anchor every shadow and highlight to its source and the object's position. Change illumination only when the light, surface, camera, or obstruction changes.

AI MISTAKE: Feet slide while bearing weight, objects float above their supports, or hands and tools intersect surfaces without any physical response. IN REALITY: A foot plants before the body moves over it. A wheel meets the road at a stable contact point. A hand pressing a cushion makes a small indentation, and a bottle set on a table settles with a slight wobble. Objects in front also block the view of objects behind them. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Establish clear contact points and correct overlap. Show weight transfer, pressure, and small surface responses; keep supported objects resting on their supports rather than hovering or passing through them.

AI MISTAKE: A moving camera carries the foreground and distant background across the frame together like a flat picture, or stationary landmarks slide independently. IN REALITY: From a moving vehicle, close roadside posts cross the view quickly while a distant ridge shifts slowly. During a camera glide above rooftops, nearby roofs move farther across the frame than the far skyline. Road edges and parallel rails narrow toward a consistent vanishing area. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Build camera movement with depth-dependent parallax. Move nearby features faster across the image than distant ones, preserve the relative positions of fixed landmarks, and keep scale and perspective consistent.

AI MISTAKE: A cut or dissolve becomes an impossible camera journey, with objects stretching or morphing to connect two separately filmed views. An image displayed on a screen may appear to occupy the surrounding room. IN REALITY: A cut simply begins a new viewpoint or moment. A dissolve temporarily blends two images without making their objects physically transform. A screen image remains within its display border, with its own texture and softness. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Treat edits as boundaries between shots, not continuous physical motion. Keep each shot spatially coherent, preserve display borders, and allow the next view to start directly without inventing an in-between action.

AI MISTAKE: Walls, windows, tiles, rails, or furniture bend, drift, or change their arrangement during one continuous shot. IN REALITY: A door moves within its frame, but the frame stays put. As a person walks down an alley, the windows, wires, and steps retain their shapes and positions relative to one another. Camera movement changes where fixed objects appear in the frame, not how they fit together. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Keep the surroundings rigid and continuous throughout the shot. Preserve the exact spacing, shape, and placement of buildings, fixtures, floor patterns, and other stationary details while the camera and people move.

AI MISTAKE: Near and distant objects become equally sharp, or background blur changes without a plausible shift in focus. IN REALITY: A lens focuses on a particular distance. A face at that distance holds clear detail while objects farther behind it soften; a writing tip can be crisp while the desk beyond it is blurred. Blur changes smoothly with distance and changes over time only when the camera or focus changes. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Hold focus on the close subject. Let objects at other depths fall progressively out of focus, and keep the focal plane consistent unless a deliberate focus shift is shown.

AI MISTAKE: Every part of the footage looks equally crisp and clean, even across great distances, darkness, rain, or rapid movement. IN REALITY: Nearby detail may be clear while distant buildings lose contrast in haze. Rain veils the background, low light reveals less fine detail, and a quick pan can smear moving edges in the direction of travel. Older-looking footage may retain grain and softness rather than flawless digital definition. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Preserve the shot’s natural limits on detail. Keep appropriate focus falloff, atmospheric softness, low-light texture, and directional motion blur instead of sharpening every subject and background surface alike.

AI MISTAKE: People or animals glide, pivot, lift, or land without planted support, momentum, or visible effort. IN REALITY: A walker transfers weight onto one foot before the other leaves the ground. A runner plants a foot and leans into a turn. A carried bag swings from its handle, lagging behind its owner’s changing pace. Lifting requires a stable stance and a shift in balance. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Show continuous, gravity-bound movement with feet that make firm contact, joints that bend in sequence, and bodies that adjust their center of mass before turning, reaching, carrying, or lifting.

AI MISTAKE: The soundtrack gains music, dialogue, machinery, calls, or emphatic effects that the recorded scene does not establish. IN REALITY: A quiet room may contain only faint ventilation and small movements. A subdued street view can have distant, indistinct traffic without a musical cue or a newly prominent speaker. Narration, when present, can pause naturally rather than punctuating each visible action. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Use only sounds supported by the setting and stated audio. Keep quiet passages quiet; do not add music, intelligible speech, dramatic effects, or synchronized noises to fill gaps in the scene.

AI MISTAKE: Background sounds sit at one constant level, with every distant voice isolated and as clear as a nearby one. IN REALITY: Corridor conversations overlap, swell as people approach, and fade as they leave. Footsteps can briefly mask a word; a nearby speaker breathes and pauses. Outdoors, occasional bird calls emerge from quieter background noise rather than repeating at regular intervals. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Build uneven, layered ambience with natural changes in distance and loudness. Let sounds overlap and sometimes mask one another. Keep distant voices indistinct instead of separating every source into clean, equally prominent audio.

AI MISTAKE: A person appears or moves their lips merely because a voice is heard, or a visible source is added to explain another off-screen sound. IN REALITY: Someone can speak from beyond the camera’s view while the frame remains on an empty hallway or a listening person. Footsteps can be audible before their source enters the shot, or without anyone entering at all. Sound does not prove that its source is visible. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Keep the stated sound off-screen. Do not introduce a new person, lip movement, object, or event unless the shot itself establishes that source in view.

AI MISTAKE: A cast shadow floats away from its object, stays fixed while the object moves, or points in a direction the lighting cannot produce. IN REALITY: A foot settling onto the ground has contact at its base, and its shadow follows its position. A tipping box changes the shape and reach of its shadow as it turns. Objects lit by the same light cast shadows in compatible directions; several lights may produce overlapping shadows. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Anchor shadows to their casting objects and receiving surfaces. Match each shadow’s position, shape, softness, and direction to the object’s movement and the scene’s lights.

AI MISTAKE: A camera pan or glide makes the whole scene slide as one flat layer, produces an unexplained zoom, or shifts the horizon without cause. IN REALITY: Viewpoint changes affect apparent positions according to depth. Nearby trees shift more against a distant hillside as the camera travels past them. When a camera retreats, more surroundings come into view and object sizes change consistently. A locked camera leaves the background still while subjects move through it. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Use physically consistent perspective and parallax for the specified camera path. Keep the horizon and fixed landmarks stable unless the camera’s actual movement explains their change.

AI MISTAKE: An observed shot becomes a smooth cinematic track, or a steady camera acquires dramatic shake, focus pulls, and reframing it never had. IN REALITY: A fixed sidewalk view holds its framing as people cross. A handheld spectator’s view may jostle, pass briefly behind a shoulder, and reframe abruptly. A distant recording retains its imperfect composition and limited detail rather than gaining an impossibly close perspective. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Follow the camera treatment specified for the shot. Keep fixed views fixed, preserve natural handheld interruptions where present, and do not add tracking, zooms, focus pulls, or exposure changes without a visible reason.

AI MISTAKE: Natural and handmade surfaces become uniformly smooth, glossy, or covered in a repeated texture, so mortar looks like paste and petals look identical. IN REALITY: Mortar has grit and small lumps, especially where it catches on a brick edge or a hand. Dough holds uneven folds and floury patches; plant fibers split at different widths; worn surfaces show marks in particular places rather than everywhere at once. Light catches raised grains and damp spots differently. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Show material-specific texture up close: gritty mortar, irregular dough folds, separated fibers, localized wear, and small highlights that follow the actual surface.

AI MISTAKE: Repeated people or objects appear identical, spotless, and evenly spaced, as though every position were measured. IN REALITY: Parked cars leave different gaps and sit at slightly different angles. Tools overlap on a work surface, cut fruit pieces differ in size, and people stand at distances shaped by what they are doing. Objects do not quietly rearrange themselves between moments: a piece stays where it was placed until something moves it. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Give repeated items varied spacing, angles, sizes, and wear; keep their positions consistent, with changes caused by visible handling or movement.

AI MISTAKE: Waves repeat the same outline, foam stays attached to a fixed spot, and falling water runs like a looping sheet. IN REALITY: Each incoming wave changes as it reaches shallow ground and individual rocks. Water splits around obstacles, throws off unequal splashes, and leaves foam patches that stretch, separate, drift, and fade. Below a waterfall, new foam forms where water strikes; older patches travel downstream. A swimmer leaves turbulence that spreads and breaks apart behind them. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Animate changing wave fronts and impact points, with foam born at collisions and carried away by the moving water.

AI MISTAKE: Flowing water hangs as a blob, travels through obstacles, or slides across a scene as one unchanging texture. IN REALITY: Gravity pulls droplets downward, while contact with rocks, hands, and floors redirects nearby flow. A stream separates around a stone and rejoins unevenly; a hand entering a pool creates ripples near the contact point and changes the reflected shapes. Thin water spreads along a floor, gathers in low spots, and breaks into smaller runs at edges. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Make water respond locally to gravity, surfaces, and obstacles, with changing droplets, ripples, reflections, and flow paths.

AI MISTAKE: A pour becomes a rigid stream, floats away from the vessel lip, or fills a cup in sudden jumps without disturbing its surface. IN REALITY: Liquid leaves the lip according to the vessel’s tilt and the amount remaining. The stream narrows as pouring slows, then stops when the vessel tips back. Where it lands, it pushes the receiving liquid aside, making small currents, ripples, and sometimes bubbles; the level rises continuously as liquid enters. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Show one connected pour from lip to container, changing stream thickness, visible impact, and a steadily rising, disturbed liquid surface.

AI MISTAKE: A walker or animal glides forward while feet or hooves slide across the ground, and the body advances without a supporting step. IN REALITY: Each foot stays planted briefly as it bears weight. The body moves over that support, then the foot lifts and swings ahead while another takes the load. Hooves follow the same need for timed contact and weight transfer, though their gait differs. On soft ground, impressions remain along the route actually taken. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Match body travel to alternating planted contacts, visible weight shifts, lifted steps, and ground marks that stay behind.

AI MISTAKE: Vehicles slide sideways, turn without steering, or change speed while their wheels, wake, and surroundings suggest a different motion. IN REALITY: A turning car follows an arc, with rotating wheels and road markings passing at a rate that fits its travel. A scooter leans into a turn and adjusts its path around others; a boat leaves a wake shaped by its movement through water. An object on a conveyor moves with the belt unless something stops it. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Keep steering, lean, wheel rotation, wake, passing scenery, and carried objects consistent with each trajectory and speed.

AI MISTAKE: Hair stays frozen during movement or swings as one solid shape, sometimes fluttering when neither the head nor the air moves. IN REALITY: Loose strands and curls follow a head turn with slight delays. Some strands brush a shoulder while others lift, separate, or fall back under their own weight. A runner’s hair responds to each change of direction and settles between movements; wind affects exposed sections differently from sheltered ones. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Animate groups of strands with varied timing, contact, and gravity, responding to the head and any visible breeze before gradually settling.

AI MISTAKE: Clothing hangs like a rigid shell, floats away from its wearer, or changes folds without any movement or contact to cause them. IN REALITY: Fabric drapes under its own weight and gathers where it meets a chair, floor, hand, or body. A hem may bunch at the floor, then lag behind when its wearer steps forward. Sleeves stretch across a bending elbow and compress on the inside of the bend; heavier cloth settles differently from thin cloth. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Give fabric material-appropriate weight, tension, persistent folds, contact compression, and delayed movement that follows its support.

AI MISTAKE: Solid subjects pass through each other or remain fully visible when something closer crosses in front. IN REALITY: A passing car briefly hides the stretch of road behind it. A person crossing in front of another hides only the covered portions, while both bodies keep their separate outlines. Someone walking around a bench changes course or stops rather than cutting through it; feet and furniture do not share the same space. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Preserve clear front-to-back ordering and solid contact, with nearer objects briefly obscuring farther ones and moving subjects navigating around obstacles.

AI MISTAKE: A face holds a broad expression while the person's attention changes, or the eyes snap between targets without a reason. Sometimes the person keeps smiling at the camera during an interaction. IN REALITY: Attention moves first: a reader glances at a line, pauses, then looks up. The eyelids, brows, and corners of the mouth change by small amounts at slightly different times. A person working at a desk looks between the task and another person, not into the lens. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Let each glance follow a visible cue; build reactions through brief eye movements and restrained, gradual facial changes.

AI MISTAKE: A cut or camera angle quietly replaces a person's features, changes a cat's markings, or alters the shape of a carried object. Even fixed structures may shift between views. IN REALITY: A person remains recognizable from the side and front; seams, buttons, and accessories stay in the same places. A cat's patches and whiskers persist as its head turns. A railing keeps its spacing and alignment when the camera moves. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Preserve the same facial features, clothing details, animal markings, prop shape, and fixed geometry across every shot and angle; change only what perspective naturally changes.

AI MISTAKE: A moving hand gains a finger, a beard edge crawls across the face, or an animal's markings rearrange after it passes behind something. Shapes may stretch and settle into a different subject. IN REALITY: Fingers keep their number, joints, and proportions while a grip changes. Facial hair stays attached to the same skin as the mouth moves. Fur patterns remain in place when an animal turns, although perspective hides or reveals different areas. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Keep anatomy and identifying features continuous through movement and occlusion; allow bending, rotation, and changing visibility, but no new parts or shifting markings.

AI MISTAKE: A fast utensil stays unnaturally crisp, or blur spreads across stationary walls and pavement as though everything moved together. Sometimes blur points away from the object's path. IN REALITY: Exposure smears the rapidly moving part along its direction of travel. A turning spatula may blur at its tip while the pan stays comparatively clear. Fixed street fixtures remain stable as a passing vehicle streaks past them. Focus is separate: a distant background can be softly out of focus without moving. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Apply directional motion blur only where speed warrants it, while preserving sharp stationary details and the chosen focus plane.

AI MISTAKE: A used street or room looks freshly polished, with identical paving, flawless concrete, and spotless cookware. Dirt becomes an even color instead of material caught in particular places. IN REALITY: Concrete has pits, patches, and repairs. Paving joints vary in width and collect grit; puddles settle in low spots. A handled pot carries uneven smudges, while mud can be glossy and soft in one patch and dry at the edge. Fabric still shows its weave beneath wear. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Give used surfaces localized scuffs, deposits, stains, repairs, and changing roughness appropriate to each material, without making every area equally dirty.

AI MISTAKE: Fabric, paper, dough, and metal share one smooth finish, with the same shine and stiffness regardless of what they are. Small folds and edges disappear. IN REALITY: Cloth bends along seams and reveals a weave under close light. Book pages curve near the spine, with thin edges visible in a stack. Dough dents under a fingertip and eases outward; worn metal reflects light across irregular scratches. These differences affect silhouettes as well as highlights. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Specify each material's own texture, thickness, flexibility, and response to pressure and light; avoid a universal glossy coating or uniformly smooth surface.

AI MISTAKE: Branches, flower clusters, and mud cracks repeat with matching shapes and tidy spacing, as if stamped from a small set of templates. Handmade marks can acquire the same mechanical rhythm. IN REALITY: Nearby branches differ in thickness and angle, and snow collects unevenly along them. Flowers within a cluster vary in size and orientation. Mud cracks branch, end, and meet at irregular intervals, with smaller divisions near some edges. Palm trunk scars are recognizable but not identical. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Build related natural forms with varied scale, gaps, direction, and texture; keep an underlying growth or drying pattern without copying individual details.

AI MISTAKE: Steam appears as a solid white ribbon, or smoke keeps the same outline while sliding across the frame. Mist or breath may appear without a visible cause. IN REALITY: Fresh vapor forms near its warm or damp source, curls into uneven wisps, then thins as it mixes with surrounding air. Older smoke drifts farther and spreads wider than new smoke. Thin patches partly veil objects behind them, while gaps remain transparent. A weak source may produce little visible vapor. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Show vapor forming at a plausible source, changing shape continuously, drifting with air movement, and dispersing with uneven transparency.

AI MISTAKE: Falling grains form a uniform curtain, dust freezes as evenly spaced dots, or crumbs vanish halfway to the ground. Particle motion may restart in an obvious loop. IN REALITY: Heavy grains follow separate arcs and land at different times. Some sand clings to a hand while finer dust spreads nearby and lingers in the air. Crumbs tumble, bounce, or settle where they fall. Brief sparks leave short streaks before fading, rather than hanging motionless. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Give particles varied sizes, paths, speeds, and lifetimes; let them emerge from a cause and continue naturally until they land, disperse, or fade.

AI MISTAKE: Flames keep one cutout shape, and bubbles appear in an evenly spaced pattern that repeats at the same speed. Heat looks like a loop pasted over the scene. IN REALITY: Flame tongues rise from hot spots, stretch, split, and vanish at different moments. Bright and dim areas shift without the whole flame moving as a rigid piece. In a heated pan, bubbles form mainly where heat reaches the liquid, grow at different rates, and collapse or rise away. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Anchor flames and bubbles to their heat source, but vary their outlines, timing, brightness, and individual lifetimes continuously.

AI MISTAKE: Rotors float away from their hubs, fixed panels spin, and linked parts stop or move at unrelated speeds while a machine supposedly runs. IN REALITY: A wheel turns around its axle while its hub stays attached; a record label and its grooves rotate together around a stationary spindle; a sewing needle rises and falls in step with the fabric feed. Hinges follow their pivots, and a compressed spring pushes back. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Keep every moving part connected to its visible pivot or linkage, maintain consistent rotation and resistance, and synchronize the needle, feed, controls, and resulting motion.

AI MISTAKE: Hair, grass, sleeves, and leaves sway as one rubber sheet, ripple without any breeze, or move independently of the bodies and branches holding them. IN REALITY: Individual strands and stems bend by different amounts and recover at different times; leaves remain attached to twigs, a sleeve folds around the moving arm, and heavier cloth responds less than a loose fringe. A sheltered patch may barely move even when exposed tips flutter. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Use a gentle, consistent breeze with local variations; keep roots and attachment points stable, let light elements flex separately, and make heavy fabric move subtly.

AI MISTAKE: A person remains visible through an opaque shoulder, a vehicle passes through a pole, or a branch disappears whenever it should hide part of an animal. IN REALITY: The nearer object blocks the farther one along the viewer's line of sight; its edge reveals and conceals different portions as the subjects or camera move. A passing shoulder briefly covers a face, while a train gradually uncovers the platform behind it. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Preserve clear foreground and background depth; keep opaque surfaces opaque, maintain consistent overlapping edges, and reveal hidden details only when the obstructing object moves aside.

AI MISTAKE: A speaker repeatedly opens and closes the mouth like a hinge, holds one expression through every phrase, or lets lips and teeth smear out of sync with the voice. IN REALITY: Lips form distinct shapes with the jaw, cheeks, and tongue; small pauses allow a breath or swallow, and the eyes occasionally shift toward the listener. Chewing follows the bite rather than imitating speech, with food kept inside the mouth. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Match varied lip and jaw shapes to the syllables, include natural pauses and restrained facial movement, and keep the mouth anatomy stable during speech or eating.

AI MISTAKE: A face jumps from neutral to delighted in one frame, freezes in a stock expression, or changes the lips while the eyes and cheeks remain motionless. IN REALITY: A reaction develops through small, coordinated changes: gaze shifts, eyelids narrow or widen, brows lift, cheeks rise, and the jaw and head settle at slightly different moments. Even a brief smile has a beginning and a release rather than a permanent fixed shape. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Build the expression gradually from the situation, preserve stable facial features, and let eyes, brows, cheeks, mouth, and head respond with subtle staggered timing.

AI MISTAKE: Fingers multiply, merge, change length, or sink into a held object; a hand may switch from one grip to another without releasing and repositioning. IN REALITY: Each hand keeps a consistent thumb and four fingers, with visible joints bending in plausible directions. Fingertips meet the phone, pencil, or handle at specific contact points, and the palm follows as the grip changes. During a clap, both hands approach and separate without interpenetrating. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Show anatomically consistent hands with distinct fingers and knuckles, believable joint bends, stable contact with objects, and continuous movement between any two hand positions.

AI MISTAKE: A restrained scene gains a storm, thick steam, dramatic camera sweep, or conspicuous action simply to make the image feel exciting. IN REALITY: A calm shoreline has modest water movement and steady light; a gently simmering pot may show small bubbles without a cloud of steam; a quiet portrait can remain nearly still. The visible setting determines what movement and effects belong there, not a desire for spectacle. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Preserve the scene's original calm scale, framing, light, and weather; add only effects supported by visible causes, and keep camera movement minimal when the shot is meant to be steady.

AI MISTAKE: A painted line bends between frames, a building gains windows, or a helmet's vents rearrange themselves as the camera moves. IN REALITY: Fixed markings and solid structures retain their geometry; any apparent change comes from perspective, lighting, or an object moving in front of them. A tree trunk stays rooted in the same place, and bridge cables remain attached at the same points even when their angle in the frame shifts. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Lock the shapes, counts, patterns, and attachment points of stationary details across the shot; allow only physically consistent perspective changes and occlusion.

AI MISTAKE: An off-screen voice causes a new person to appear, narration makes a silent subject speak, or a sound cue produces weather or activity absent from the visible setting. IN REALITY: Audio can come from outside the frame or be laid over the scene; a person can continue reading silently while someone else talks, and fish can swim in an aquarium beneath unrelated narration. Only visible causes should create visible actions. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Keep voiceover and off-screen sound separate from the pictured action; do not invent a speaker, movement, weather, or objects unless the shot itself establishes them.

AI MISTAKE: A foot crosses sand without an impression, a boat cuts through water without a wake, or spilled water rests on cloth and pavement without changing either surface. IN REALITY: Contact has a local, material-specific effect: sand compresses beneath weight, water parts and trails behind a moving hull, wet cloth darkens and sags, and damp concrete develops darker patches. The effect follows the point of contact and matches its force and scale. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Show localized, physically sized impressions, ripples, folds, absorption, or darkening wherever the subject touches or wets a surface; let those changes persist naturally.

names: lamp posts along a hazy street
body: AI MISTAKE: Distant cars and lamp posts look as sharp and contrasty as nearby ones, or the whole scene receives one flat dusty tint. Sunsets and clouds may have hard edges and the same saturated color everywhere. IN REALITY: Airborne dust accumulates along the line of sight. Farther objects lose fine detail and contrast gradually, while nearby edges remain clearer. At sunset, the warmest glow gathers near the horizon; the upper sky is usually quieter. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Show progressive atmospheric haze down the road, with distant cars and lamp posts increasingly soft and pale, clear foreground detail, and a concentrated warm horizon glow.

AI MISTAKE: Reflective surfaces show flawless copies, reflections that disagree with nearby objects, or glare that stays fixed regardless of viewpoint. Wet ground may look like a perfect mirror even where its surface is uneven. IN REALITY: A reflection depends on the surface angle, shape, and roughness. Curved surfaces bend reflected shapes; rippled puddles break them into shifting fragments. On clear glass, a faint reflection can overlap the view through it without replacing that view. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Keep reflections aligned with the objects and viewing angle; distort them across curved glass, break them across rippled water, and preserve visible detail behind transparent surfaces.

AI MISTAKE: Clear glass turns opaque, objects seen through it keep the wrong shape, or a reflection remains in place when its source or viewpoint changes. Layered glass and liquid boundaries merge into one impossible surface. IN REALITY: Light changes direction at glass and water boundaries, slightly shifting what appears behind them. A double-walled glass has two visible rims, and a tilted display catches different reflections as its angle changes. Transparency still reveals the geometry beyond the surface. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Preserve the scene visible through the glass; show subtle viewpoint-correct refraction at its edges, distinct boundaries for each glass layer, and reflections that track the display angle.

AI MISTAKE: Rain falls as a uniform curtain, fog moves as one solid sheet, and water or leaves repeat an identical loop. Every ripple may start and stop together. IN REALITY: Weather and flowing water vary from place to place. Small ripples overlap and travel at different rates; foam separates around rocks and reforms downstream. Passing fog briefly hides one section of a ridge while revealing another. Wind reaches leaves unevenly, so some move before their neighbors. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Animate irregular, locally changing rain, fog, and water; let ripples overlap, foam flow around obstacles, and nearby foliage respond at slightly different moments.

AI MISTAKE: A person or vehicle glides across the scene without steps, wheel rotation, steering, or a visible push. Speed changes abruptly, while tracks and dust fail to follow the route. IN REALITY: Travel has a source of force and a sequence of weight shifts. A skater pushes off one foot, recovers, and leans into a turn. A car turns along its heading; its wheels roll, its tracks curve, and disturbed dust trails behind rather than leading it. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Match each change in position to foot pushes or rolling wheels, show plausible leaning and steering, and keep tracks and dust consistent with the traveled path.

AI MISTAKE: A limb swings on its own, a torso bends at one sharp point, or a reach stretches an arm while the shoulders and hips remain frozen. Gestures can look stiff even when the hand reaches the right place. IN REALITY: Connected joints share a movement. Reaching overhead raises and rotates the shoulder and adjusts the torso; bending sideways changes the line of the neck, shoulders, waist, and hips. Planted feet continue to support the body's weight. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Animate the reach or bend through connected joints, with small compensating shifts in the torso and hips, natural joint limits, and steady support through planted feet.

AI MISTAKE: Connected pieces drift apart, pass through their supports, or move on unrelated paths. A page may spin freely instead of turning from its spine, and a hanging seat may move without its supports. IN REALITY: Attachments constrain motion. A page flexes outward from the book's spine while the book stays put. A bracelet follows the wrist with a little play; a swing seat follows the arc allowed by its hanging points. Loose clothing can lag behind the main movement. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Keep each part anchored at its actual attachment, maintain believable distance and tension, and let flexible portions lag or bend without detaching.

AI MISTAKE: Cloth, hair, and paper travel like solid boards, or they flutter endlessly without a touch or breeze. Folds appear and disappear without following the material. IN REALITY: Flexible materials bend under their own weight and resist changes in shape. A lifted towel sags between the hands and forms folds as it settles. Paper flexes near its corners before lying flat. Hair strands lag behind a head movement and then gradually come to rest. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Give each material its own bend and settling behavior; let gravity shape towels, corners flex on paper, and individual hair strands respond briefly to movement before resting.

AI MISTAKE: Straps and ribbons float beside their attachments, stretch without resistance, or pass through the body. A sleeve may keep the same folds while the arm bends, and a cord may flap despite still air. IN REALITY: An accessory has weight, an attachment point, and material-specific give. A strap sags when slack and straightens when pulled. A ribbon flutters in moving air, then falls back; a sleeve gathers at the elbow as the arm bends. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Anchor every strap, cord, and garment to its support; show slack sagging, taut sections pulling, and folds or flutter responding to actual movement and airflow.

AI MISTAKE: A resting subject constantly turns, sways, or repeats an obvious head movement just to keep the frame active. A sleeping animal may perform the same large gesture every few seconds. IN REALITY: Quiet subjects can remain nearly still for a meaningful interval. Breathing may be subtle; a cat might adjust an ear once, and a perched bird might make a small head correction before settling again. These movements are occasional rather than rhythmic loops. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Hold a calm, mostly still pose for several seconds, with restrained breathing and only sparse, small ear, eye, or head adjustments at irregular moments.

AI MISTAKE: A cut, crease, or drilled hole appears instantly, while the hand and tool barely move and the material shows no resistance. IN REALITY: A knife presses into food before the blade travels through it and the pieces separate; fingers push dough into a fold that remains creased; a drill bit advances gradually, lifting irregular chips from the wood. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Show the complete tool path in sequence, including initial contact, pressure, visible material deformation, gradual separation or penetration, and small displaced fragments; keep the hand, tool, and changing material aligned throughout the action.

AI MISTAKE: Text and digits turn into gibberish, duplicate across unrelated displays, or change without input; content may even appear on the hidden side of a device. IN REALITY: A phone viewed from behind shows its casing and rear cameras, not its screen; printed letters stay fixed to their surface, an idle visible display stays stable, and separate monitors can show different coherent views. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Respect which display surfaces face the camera, keep readable content attached to each surface and consistent between frames, and change on-screen values only after a visible input or a clearly established live update.

AI MISTAKE: Separate people, grass stems, droplets, or fingers move on the same beat, repeat identical cycles, and reverse direction together. IN REALITY: Neighbors respond to slightly different forces and timings: stems bend by different amounts, droplets fall along distinct paths, and people vary their step lengths while adjusting around one another. Even repeated gestures have small changes in speed and reach. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Give each independently moving subject its own timing, path, and amplitude; allow brief pauses and imperfect overlaps, while keeping shared environmental forces, such as a gust of wind, evident without making every response identical.

AI MISTAKE: A generator adds a clearly visible object, movement, or source merely because the scene label or soundtrack suggests one, even when the camera view does not establish it. IN REALITY: A distant field can leave a small ball indistinct; a plated dish can remain completely still; a sound from outside the frame need not reveal its source. The image is limited by framing, distance, occlusion, and what the camera can resolve. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Depict only what this shot visibly establishes; keep distant details ambiguous when too small to read, leave still objects still, and let off-screen sounds remain off-screen.

AI MISTAKE: Every window, lamp, tent, and stretch of pavement glows at the same brightness, making a night scene look evenly filled with light. IN REALITY: Each source illuminates a limited area; surfaces facing it brighten, nearby objects cast shadows, and recesses remain dark. A bright bulb or flame may lose visible detail at its center, while the ground several steps away receives much less light. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Place distinct local light sources with believable falloff, uneven pools of illumination, dark gaps between them, and restrained reflections that appear only on surfaces positioned to catch the light.

AI MISTAKE: An unusual camera position stretches limbs, changes equipment size, or bends solid surroundings instead of producing ordinary perspective. IN REALITY: A hand close to the lens can appear larger than a distant shoulder, but its joints still connect in a plausible order; rigid objects retain coherent edges, and repeated features shrink consistently with distance. Camera tilt changes the view, not the underlying anatomy or construction. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Specify the camera height, angle, and distance; allow normal perspective enlargement near the lens, while preserving connected body proportions, rigid-object geometry, and consistent scale cues across the scene.

AI MISTAKE: A wet road becomes a perfectly sharp, continuous mirror, and its reflected scene stays fixed as the viewpoint or subject moves. IN REALITY: Asphalt texture interrupts reflections, shallow puddles form separate smoother patches, and ripples or passing tires disturb the image. A reflected object changes position and shape with camera angle, water depth, and surface roughness; some dark areas show no recognizable reflection at all. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Break reflections across granular pavement, reserve clearer inverted shapes for calm puddles, vary sharpness from patch to patch, and update reflected positions consistently when the camera or subject moves.

AI MISTAKE: Rain or washing coats every surface with an identical glossy layer, with no dry patches, runoff, or visible boundary between wet and unwet areas. IN REALITY: Drops bead on some materials and spread on others; water collects in low spots, runs down slopes, and leaves streaks beneath edges. Sheltered areas can stay dry while exposed ground darkens unevenly, and reflections appear only where the water and viewing angle permit them. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Vary wetness by material, shelter, slope, and contact with water; show irregular beads, streaks, pooling, patchy sheen, and a waterline that follows the surface.

AI MISTAKE: A surface becomes featurelessly smooth or fills with cloned marks, identical stones, and regularly spaced imperfections. IN REALITY: Pebbles differ in size, shape, orientation, and color; their appearance also shifts beneath shallow water. Manufactured surfaces have structure, but seams, scuffs, and worn areas do not repeat with perfect spacing across the whole frame. Fine detail changes with distance and illumination rather than remaining equally crisp everywhere. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Preserve the material’s recognizable grain while varying individual features; include occasional clusters and gaps, local wear, scale changes in perspective, and a visible color shift where dry ground passes under water.

AI MISTAKE: Food and working materials look uniformly smooth or behave as though they have the wrong thickness, powderiness, or stickiness. IN REALITY: Flour gathers unevenly on damp fish and transfers in small patches to fingers; thick sauce clings to a spoon before sliding off; glue stays concentrated where applied and can form short strands as joined surfaces pull apart. Residue remains at contact points rather than appearing everywhere at once. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Describe the material’s specific consistency and contact behavior, including uneven coating, plausible buildup, small transfers to hands or tools, and residue limited to surfaces the material actually touched.

AI MISTAKE: Faces look polished like plastic, with pores, fine stubble, tiny creases, and changes in skin tension erased. IN REALITY: Skin has uneven texture even in soft light. A smile gathers small folds beside the eyes and mouth, while a head turn changes the folds under the chin and along the neck. Stubble catches light differently across the jaw, and cheeks do not remain perfectly smooth as they move. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Show natural skin texture at a flattering distance, with visible pores, subtle stubble, and facial and neck creases that change naturally when the person turns or smiles.

AI MISTAKE: Every person or animal keeps moving at the same speed, starts and stops together, or crosses the frame without a natural hesitation. IN REALITY: A pedestrian slows to make room, another pauses to look at a stall, and someone nearer the camera briefly hides a person behind them. Companions adjust their steps without matching perfectly. Animals pause, turn their heads, then move again. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Give each figure an independent pace, with brief stops, small changes of direction, and natural overlaps as foreground figures pass in front of those farther away.

AI MISTAKE: Clouds, waves, or ripples slide across the scene as one rigid sheet, repeating the same shapes at a constant speed. IN REALITY: Nearby ripples spread and fade while wider swells arrive beneath them. Cloud edges soften, stretch, and change shape; thin high clouds can drift differently from thicker low ones. No single pattern stays intact across the whole frame. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Show overlapping environmental patterns at several scales, with independent speeds and gently changing shapes. Let small water ripples appear and disappear among broader waves, and let separate cloud layers evolve rather than scroll.

AI MISTAKE: Steam, dust, snow, or rain forms an evenly spaced screen, a fixed overlay, or an oversized effect with no visible source. IN REALITY: Steam rises from warm water in uneven wisps, thickening over one part of a pool before drifting aside and revealing it again. Dust is easiest to see in a shaft of light. Falling particles vary in spacing and depth, and nearer ones may briefly cross the view. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Place atmospheric particles where their source and lighting support them, with uneven density, varied depth, and natural gaps rather than a uniform layer.

AI MISTAKE: Bubbles and droplets appear identical and evenly spaced, foam repeats its pattern, or liquid details travel in directions their weight and surroundings cannot support. IN REALITY: Droplets gather where moisture runs, merge into larger drops, and follow a sloping path. Bubbles cluster and change size around vegetables moving in a pan. Foam breaks into patches, while steam curls upward in irregular wisps. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Vary the size, spacing, and lifetime of each bubble or drop. Make droplets collect and descend along the surface, and let bubbles and steam respond to the food and heat.

AI MISTAKE: A landing ends without slowing the moving object, or a cushion stays perfectly still when something settles onto it. IN REALITY: Motion changes at contact. A person landing on a mattress bends slightly as it gives way, then steadies. A ball dents a soft cushion for a moment before it rebounds, while a bag makes a seat dip and settle. The reaction begins where the surfaces touch, not across the whole scene at once. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Show clear deceleration at contact, local compression in the receiving surface, and a small, properly timed rebound or settling motion.

AI MISTAKE: A vehicle glides sideways while its wheels remain still, or a machine attachment changes position without its connected joints moving. IN REALITY: Rolling wheels match the distance traveled, and a turning truck follows a curved path set by its steering wheels. An excavator bucket changes angle as the boom and stick articulate in sequence. The body may lean or settle slightly, but its parts stay connected and support the motion. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Coordinate wheel rotation, steering angle, and travel path. For machinery, animate each linked joint so the attachment reaches its new position through plausible articulation.

AI MISTAKE: Cars overlap, drift across lane markings, or stream through an intersection at one unchanging pace regardless of the signal. IN REALITY: Drivers leave visible space, slow into a queue, and wait behind the marked stopping point. When their signal changes, the first vehicles move off and the others follow with short delays. Turning vehicles trace their own paths, while pedestrians cross during an appropriate pause in traffic. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Keep each vehicle in a consistent lane with clear separation. Show signal-controlled groups stopping, waiting, and moving through the junction in a believable sequence.

AI MISTAKE: A swing moves at constant speed through its arc, a foot slips off a turning pedal, or a rope moves independently of the part it pulls. IN REALITY: A swing slows near the top, reverses, and moves fastest near the bottom. A bicycle pedal carries the rider’s foot around with its crank. A taut rope changes position as its pulley turns and the attached load moves. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Time each connected part together. Preserve contact between foot and pedal, match rope travel to pulley rotation, and give a swinging object a natural slowdown and reversal.

AI MISTAKE: Hair merges into the background, holds a hard solid outline, or moves as one stiff piece when the head turns. IN REALITY: Individual strands remain visible against a contrasting background, while thicker locks retain their shape without becoming rigid. Wind lifts some hairs before others. During a head turn, loose ends lag briefly behind the scalp and settle at different times. Light catches flyaway strands along the edge of the hair. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Keep a clear, detailed hair silhouette with fine stray strands, separate moving locks, and subtle delayed motion after each head turn or gust.

AI MISTAKE: A person speaking repeats the same mouth opening and closing cycle while both hands wave continuously, regardless of what is being said. IN REALITY: Lips and cheeks form different shapes across a phrase. The mouth settles briefly at pauses, and a hand may lift to emphasize one point, then rest while the next sentence continues. Small head movements and blinks occur at their own pace rather than on every syllable. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Show natural conversational timing: varied lip and cheek movement matched to phrases, brief still pauses, and occasional short hand gestures that begin and end without looping.

AI MISTAKE: A breaking object bends like rubber, fades away, or turns into an indistinct cloud instead of separating into material-specific pieces. IN REALITY: Paper resists briefly, then tears along a jagged path shaped by its fibers, leaving two physical edges. Safety glass separates into many small pieces that fall and scatter. A brittle tile sheds hard fragments from the point where it gives way; those fragments remain visible after they land. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Keep the material recognizable throughout the break, with the tear or fracture starting at the contact point and persistent pieces moving under gravity.

AI MISTAKE: Pencil marks appear ahead of the moving tip, slide around on the page, or emerge as perfectly even lines despite changes in hand pressure. IN REALITY: The pencil leaves graphite only where its tip contacts the paper. A stroke grows behind the tip as the hand moves; it stops when the tip lifts. Pressure, angle, and the paper's texture make some stretches darker or wider than others. Earlier marks stay fixed on the page while the hand moves around them. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Track each new graphite mark precisely under the contacting pencil tip, with subtle pressure variation and no shifting of completed strokes.

AI MISTAKE: Spray appears before a pump is pressed, or one quick brush or dab instantly completes a change that should build through repeated contact. IN REALITY: A finger pushes the pump down before droplets emerge from the nozzle. The mist travels outward and settles over a short interval. A brush changes only the section of hair it passes through; cream covers the areas touched by the fingers, then spreads with later passes. Each visible result follows its initiating motion. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Preserve the order of contact, release, travel, and accumulation; let each pass change only the area it reaches.

AI MISTAKE: A topping covers an entire surface the instant a spoon touches it, or a shaped piece of clay returns to its old form between shots without being handled. IN REALITY: Topping first gathers where it lands, then spreads outward under the spoon, leaving visible edges and thicker patches. Clay deforms beneath the fingers and retains its new contours after the hands pull away. Untouched areas remain as they were until another pass reaches them. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Make changes local and cumulative, show the tool moving material from one place to another, and preserve every resulting shape across consecutive moments.

AI MISTAKE: Background people stand frozen, walk in identical loops, or reappear as matching copies, while vehicles hold their positions like painted scenery. IN REALITY: One pedestrian crosses the frame while another pauses near a stall; others move at different speeds and in different directions. A distant vehicle advances behind nearby people and becomes partly hidden as it passes. Background motion is modest but continuous, with no synchronized steps or duplicated outfits and faces. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Give each visible bystander and vehicle an independent, plausible path with varied timing, natural occlusion, and consistent appearance from frame to frame.

AI MISTAKE: A ball passes through a rim or net without touching anything, or net cords stay stiff and cut visibly through the ball. IN REALITY: The rim remains fixed. When the ball meets the net, nearby cords bend around its surface and pull taut, slightly slowing its descent. As the ball clears them, the cords flick back and sway for a moment before settling. The ball and cords never occupy the same solid space. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Show contact at the correct point, with local cord tension, brief ball slowdown, and a small trailing net sway after release.

AI MISTAKE: A vehicle's body stretches as it turns, chair legs change length during a camera move, or equipment seams drift apart between views. IN REALITY: Rigid parts keep their dimensions and stay joined at the same points. Their visible outlines change with perspective, not because the object itself melts or expands. A turning chair may reveal a previously hidden leg, but its seat, frame, and joints retain stable proportions. WRITE IT LIKE THIS: Keep the object's structure locked across movement and viewpoint changes; allow only perspective, occlusion, and genuine joint motion to change what the camera sees.
